title: Fast & slow pointers
summary: Move one pointer one step and another two steps. When the fast one reaches the end, the slow one is in the middle; if they meet, there is a cycle.
idea: The fast pointer covers twice the distance, so the slow one is always halfway. In a loop the fast one gains one step per move and must catch up.

signals.see: You need the middle of a linked list in one pass.
signals.think: slow moves 1, fast moves 2. When fast runs out, slow is at the middle.

signals.see: You must tell whether a list, or a chain of next-values, loops back on itself.
signals.think: Run slow and fast. If they ever meet, there is a cycle; if fast hits the end, there is none.

signals.see: You need the k-th node from the end without counting the length first.
signals.think: Move a lead pointer k steps ahead, then move both one step at a time until the lead hits the end.

signals.see: The question limits you to O(1) extra space where a set of seen nodes would be easy.
signals.think: Two pointers replace the set: the meeting point proves a cycle without storing anything.

phrasings: A playlist is a linked list. Which song is exactly in the middle?
Each page links to a next page. Does following the links ever bring you back to a page you saw?
Remove the third-last stop from a linked list of bus stops in a single pass.

picture.title: Two speeds, one pass
picture.alt: On the left, the list is walked once to count the nodes and again to stop halfway. On the right, a slow pointer moves one step and a fast pointer two steps, so when the fast pointer ends the slow one is at the middle after a single pass.
picture.caption: Fast covers twice the ground, so slow is always halfway.

code.py:
def middle_node(head):
    slow = fast = head  #@init
    while fast and fast['next']:  #@loop
        slow = slow['next']  #@slow
        fast = fast['next']['next']  #@fast
    return slow['val']  #@done

visualiser.inputHelp: 1 to 12 list values between -99 and 99, separated by commas.

oneLiner: slow = fast = head; while fast and fast.next: slow 1 step, fast 2; meet → cycle

exercise.prompt: Remove the middle node of the list and return the head. With an even number of nodes, remove the second of the two middle nodes. A one-node list becomes empty (null). The starter already stops slow just before the middle node, but never unlinks it. Finish it.
hints: Starting fast two nodes ahead makes slow stop one node early, right before the middle.
Skip the middle node: set slow.next to slow.next.next.

complexity.why: fast reaches the end after about n / 2 moves. In a cycle, fast gains one step per move, so they meet within one lap. Only two pointers are stored.

mistakes: Checking only fast.next and not fast, which crashes when fast is already null.
Starting both pointers in a way that gives the first middle when the question wants the second (or the reverse).
Comparing values instead of nodes when testing for a meeting. Different nodes can hold the same value.
For the start of a cycle, forgetting the second phase: reset one pointer to the head and move both one step at a time.

quiz.question: slow and fast start at the head of a 6-node list. Where is slow when the loop ends?
quiz.explain: fast stops after 3 jumps (at null), and slow has moved 3 steps, landing on the 4th node: the second middle.

quiz.question: Why must fast eventually meet slow if there is a cycle?
choices: Fast gets one step closer every move, so the gap reaches zero
Both pointers stop at the tail
quiz.explain: Inside the loop the gap shrinks by exactly one each move, so it cannot jump over slow.

quiz.question: You want the 2nd node from the end in one pass. What setup works?
choices: Move a lead pointer 2 steps ahead, then move both until the lead is null
quiz.explain: With a gap of 2, when the lead walks off the end the trailing pointer is on the 2nd-last node.

interviewTip: Trace the pointers on lists of length 1, 2 and 3 out loud. Those tiny cases settle which middle you return and catch null checks before the interviewer does.
